h1: SEO for HR tech in a category buyers search by statute
metaTitle: SEO for HR Tech: Compliance Search Wins
metaDescription: SEO for HR tech companies in India: rank the PF, ESI, gratuity and Form 16 queries HR teams search, attach a calculator, then route them to the product.
answer: HR tech buyers in India search for statutory deadlines long before they search for software. PF, ESI, gratuity, Form 16 and payroll compliance queries pull HR and finance teams onto your site at a volume feature pages never reach. Rank those, attach a calculator or template, then route to the product.
takeaways: Indian payroll runs on statute. Statute creates deadlines, deadlines create search, and that demand already exists — you don't have to manufacture it with category explainers.
The best-performing asset in HR tech is almost never an article. It's a **calculator or a template** the HR team needs before Wednesday's payroll run.
Statutory pages decay faster than anything else you publish. Date them visibly and schedule the review, or they become a live demonstration that your compliance product doesn't keep up.
SMB and enterprise are two keyword sets wearing one category name. One page set cannot serve both, and blended reporting hides which one is working.

sections.h2: Your buyer searches for a deadline before they search for a product
body: An HR manager at a 300-person company does not wake up wanting an HRMS. She wakes up because Form 16 has to go out, a PF challan is due, or finance has asked why the gratuity provision moved. That is the query she types. It has nothing to do with your product name and everything to do with whether she lands on your site or a competitor's.

This is the structural advantage HR tech has over most software categories. A page titled 'what is an HRMS' competes with fifty near-identical pages and attracts students. A page that explains the EPF contribution split correctly, with the arithmetic shown, attracts the person who eventually signs the invoice — and the payroll executive who tells her which tool to shortlist.

callout.title: The trap on the other side of that advantage
callout.body: Statutory content decays faster than anything else you publish. Wage ceilings move, forms get renumbered, states notify their own rules on their own timetable, and the four labour codes have been rolling out in stages. A payroll page carrying last year's numbers is worse than no page — it publicly demonstrates that your compliance product doesn't keep up. Put a visible 'last reviewed' date on every statutory page and a real review cycle in someone's calendar.

body: Four query families do most of the work. They aren't equal. Some bring HR ops, some bring finance, and some bring employees who will never buy anything — but who link, share, and get your page quoted in an AI answer about Indian payroll.

table.caption: Statutory query families in Indian payroll and what each page has to contain.
head: Query family
Who is actually searching
What the page must contain
rows: EPF and PF — rates, withdrawal, UAN, challan
HR ops and employees, in roughly equal measure
The 12% employee and 12% employer contribution, how the employer share splits between the pension and provident components, the ₹15,000 statutory wage ceiling, and a worked example in rupees.
ESI — eligibility, contribution, benefits
HR ops at companies sitting near the threshold
The ₹21,000 gross wage limit, the 0.75% employee and 3.25% employer split, which establishments are covered, and what happens when an employee crosses the limit mid-contribution-period.
Gratuity — eligibility, calculation, tax
Employees first, finance second
The five-year continuous service rule, the last-drawn-salary × 15/26 × years formula, the tax-exempt ceiling, and a calculator that runs the number for them.
Form 16, TDS and professional tax
HR in May, employees in June and July
Part A versus Part B, what to reconcile against Form 26AS and the AIS before filing, and the fact that professional tax is a state subject with different slabs and different due dates.

bullets: **Write for the person, not the persona.** An employee searching 'how to withdraw PF online' is not your buyer, but they are the reason the page earns links. Serve them properly and your buyer-facing pages inherit the authority.
**Show the arithmetic.** Every one of these queries has a number at the end of it. A page that explains the rule and refuses to run an example loses to the page that runs it.
**Put the effective date on the page, not in a schema field nobody reads.** 'Rates as applicable from [date]' at the top costs a line and buys credibility with both readers and reviewers.

sections.h2: Templates and calculators do the lead capture your blog can't
body: The best-performing asset in HR tech SEO is rarely an article. It's a thing the HR team downloads on a Tuesday because payroll runs on Wednesday: an offer letter format, a salary structure sheet, a full-and-final settlement template, a gratuity calculator, a CTC-to-in-hand breakdown.

These work for two reasons. They sit at the exact moment of need, and they are linkable in a way a 2,000-word guide isn't. Another HR blog will link to your gratuity calculator. Nobody links to your gratuity article.
bullets: **Don't gate the first interaction.** An email wall on the calculator kills the links that make it rank. Capture on the result screen instead — 'email me this breakdown' converts better than a gate, because the person already has the value.
**Ship templates in the format they actually use.** Excel and Google Sheets. Not a PDF of a screenshot of a spreadsheet.
**One page per template, never a downloads hub.** A hub ranks for nothing. Fifteen separate pages rank for fifteen separate queries and carry fifteen separate sets of links.
**Instrument them.** Track which downloads precede a demo request. You will usually find a short list of assets doing most of the pipeline work — find yours before you build the sixteenth.

sections.h2: Feature and integration pages that read like a product, not a brochure
body: Two page types carry the middle of an HR tech funnel, and both are usually written by whoever had capacity that sprint.
One page per module — payroll, attendance, leave, onboarding, performance, ATS — each written against the query patterns `[module] software` and `[module] software for [segment]`.

The failure mode is six pages that are the same page with the module name swapped. If your leave management page could be turned into your attendance page with find and replace, Google is right to pick one and ignore the rest. That's [keyword cannibalization](/glossary/keyword-cannibalization) with extra steps, and it's why your feature pages plateau.

Indian HR stacks are held together by accounting software and biometric devices. `[your product] Tally integration`, `[your product] Zoho Books integration`, `[your product] biometric attendance integration` — every pairing is a query with a buyer at the end of it who is already paying for one side of it.

A real page per integration — what syncs, what doesn't, how the field mapping works, what breaks at month-end close — is programmatic SEO nobody can call thin, because each page describes a genuinely different system. That's the distinction we've written about in [where programmatic SEO crosses the scaled content line](/journal/programmatic-seo-and-the-scaled-content-line): templating is fine, publishing pages nobody would miss is not.

sections.h2: Comparison pages in a category where everyone claims full compliance
body: Every HRMS sold in India says it handles PF, ESI, professional tax and TDS. Buyers know that's the claim, and they search for the comparison anyway: `X vs Y`, `X alternatives`, `best payroll software for startups`. Somebody is going to own those pages. It may as well be the vendor telling the truth on them.
bullets: **Compare on the things that genuinely differ**: how many states are supported for professional tax, whether challans are generated or merely calculated, multi-entity handling, how a mid-period ESI threshold change is treated, API limits, and what implementation actually costs on top of the licence.

**Name who should buy the other product.** A comparison page that concedes nothing gets screenshotted in your competitor's sales channel and cited by nobody. A fair one gets linked, and increasingly gets quoted by AI assistants, which summarise pages that read as neutral.
**Keep the pricing rows current or delete them.** A stale price on a comparison page is the fastest way to lose a deal you were winning.
**Don't compare against a product you've never run.** It shows. In a category this small, the other vendor's team will point it out to your prospect.

callout.title: Where the category comparison sits
callout.body: Comparison and alternatives pages have the highest purchase intent of anything you can rank for, and the smallest volume. Do not judge them on traffic. Judge them on demo requests per hundred sessions, where they will beat your best blog post by an order of magnitude.

sections.h2: SMB and enterprise are two keyword sets pretending to be one
body: A 40-person startup and a 4,000-person manufacturer both search 'HR software India'. Only one of them is your customer, and if you sell to both you need two page sets — not one page with a segment dropdown.

bullets: Separate templates, separate internal linking, separate calls to action, separate reporting. Blending them produces pages that half-address both and convert neither.

Report keyword → landing page → signup or demo → qualified. A report built on sessions tells you nothing here, because the enterprise set will always look like a rounding error on traffic and carry most of the revenue.

faqs.q: Does payroll compliance content actually bring software buyers, or just employees?
faqs.a: Both, and the split depends on the query. Withdrawal and calculation queries skew heavily towards employees; challan, filing deadline, return and multi-state queries skew towards HR ops and finance — the people who shortlist vendors. The employee traffic still earns the links that make the buyer-facing pages rank.

faqs.q: How often should statutory HR content be updated?
faqs.a: At every rate, threshold or form change, plus a scheduled sweep at the start of the financial year in April when most slabs and state notifications land. Anything with a rupee figure in it needs an owner and a review date. A wrong number on a compliance page costs more trust than the page ever earned.

faqs.q: Are free calculators worth building for an HR tech product?
faqs.a: Yes, and they are usually the highest-return asset on the site. Gratuity, CTC-to-in-hand, PF and HRA calculators sit exactly at the moment of need, attract links from other HR blogs, and put your product in front of somebody mid-task. Build them ungated and capture the email on the result.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to produce pipeline for an HR tech company?
faqs.a: Four to eight months in most cases, and the range is wide because it depends on your existing domain authority more than on the content. Statutory pages on an established domain can rank inside two months. The same pages on a young domain wait for links first, which is the slow part.
